Puritan
PYOOR-ih-tun
noun / adjective
From Latin puritas (purity, from purus, pure, clean, undefiled). The term “Puritan” began as a term of derision applied by opponents to those within the Elizabethan Church of England who pressed for further reform on biblical principles, particularly the purification of worship according to the regulative principle. By the mid-seventeenth century it had attached itself to the broad Reformed orthodox movement in England and New England associated with Westminster-standard Calvinism, complementarian household order, rigorous piety, and the subordination of all life to Scripture.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Puritans were not a formal denomination but a transatlantic Reformed movement (c. 1560–1700) united by the conviction that the English Reformation had been incomplete — that the Church of England retained too many ceremonies, vestments, episcopal structures, and worship practices inherited from Rome rather than commanded by Scripture. They pressed for the full application of the regulative principle of worship (worship is governed by what Scripture commands, not what tradition allows), the sovereignty of God in election and providence (Calvinist soteriology), the authority of the Bible over every domain of life, and the cultivation of a disciplined, Christ-centered piety in family, vocation, and civil life. Their theological output — Richard Sibbes, William Perkins, Thomas Goodwin, John Owen, Thomas Watson, Richard Baxter, Matthew Henry — remains among the richest in Protestant history. The Westminster Confession of Faith (1647) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession represent the doctrinal apex of the Puritan theological project. Puritan piety emphasized the covenant of grace operating through the family unit (household worship, catechesis of children, spousal covenant), the mortification of sin by the Spirit's power, the weekly keeping of the Lord's Day as a Christian Sabbath, and the preaching of the Word as the primary means of grace. Their approach to Scripture, the soul, and the Christian life has been called the “school of Christ” — and the recovery of Puritan theology (J. I. Packer, Martyn Lloyd-Jones, the Banner of Truth Trust) has been the defining feature of robust evangelical Calvinism since the mid-twentieth century.

Webster 1828 Definition

A member or adherent of the English and American Reformed movement (c. 1560–1700) that sought the thorough reformation of the church and personal life on the basis of Scripture alone — characterized by Calvinist soteriology, the regulative principle of worship, rigorous household piety, and Sabbath observance.

expand to see more

PURITAN, n. [L. puritas, purity.] In church history: one of the strict English Calvinists of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries who, not content with the Elizabethan religious settlement, pressed for further reformation of the church in doctrine, worship, polity, and life according to Scripture alone.

2. A member of the broad Reformed-orthodox movement in England (c. 1560–1700) and New England (c. 1620–1700) united by Westminster-standard Calvinism, the regulative principle of worship, rigorous piety, household covenant, and the preaching of the Word as the primary means of grace.

3. The Puritan library: Richard Sibbes (Bruised Reed, 1630), William Perkins (A Golden Chain, 1591), John Owen (Death of Death, 1648; Mortification of Sin, 1656), Thomas Watson (A Body of Divinity, 1692), Matthew Henry (Commentary on the Bible, 1710) — the richest corpus of practical Reformed divinity in the English language.

4. The Puritan household: family worship, catechism of children (Westminster Shorter Catechism), spousal covenant, vocational stewardship, Sabbath observance, and the cruciform ordering of domestic life under the headship of God.

5. Recovery: the twentieth-century Puritan revival (Lloyd-Jones, Packer, Banner of Truth Trust) recovered the Puritan library for a generation starved of doctrinal depth, introducing evangelical readers to Owen on sin, Goodwin on Christ's heart, and Sibbes on grace as the medicine of a wounded conscience.

Modern Corruption

The word “Puritan” has been reduced in popular usage to a caricature of joyless, repressive, pleasure-denying religiosity — exactly inverting the Puritans' actual theology of God as the author of all true joy and the Christian life as the recovery of creational delight through the Spirit's sanctification.

expand to see more

H. L. Mencken's famous barb — “Puritanism is the haunting fear that someone, somewhere, may be happy” — has become the standard cultural gloss on the word, and it could not be more wrong. The Puritans were some of the most joyful, domestic, Word-saturated, and earnestly human of all theologians. Richard Sibbes wrote with such tender warmth toward the bruised and doubting that he was called “the heavenly Doctor.” Matthew Henry's commentary breathes gratitude on every page. John Owen's tract on communion with God is a meditation on the soul's warmest spiritual pleasures. The caricature of Puritan dourness is the libel of those who neither read nor understood them.

The progressive evangelical temptation is to dismiss the Puritan heritage as patriarchal, culturally conditioned, and therefore expendable — to replace their exegetically rigorous, confessionally precise, experientially deep piety with a therapeutic, feeling-led, doctrine-light spirituality that would have horrified them. The Puritans' answer is in their texts: own a Perkins, a Watson, a Sibbes, an Owen. Read them. The experiential depth, doctrinal precision, and pastoral warmth of the Puritan library is not an inheritance to be discarded but a treasury to be plundered for the recovery of the church's spiritual health.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The term arose from Latin puritas (purity) as a polemical nickname for those pressing Reformation thoroughness, but the Puritans embraced the concept if not always the name — understanding their project as the full application of Scripture to the purification of worship, life, and thought.

expand to see more

Latin puritas — purity, cleanness; the conceptual root — the Puritans sought the purity of church, worship, and life according to the Word alone

Regulative principle — the Puritan hermeneutic of worship: only what God commands in Scripture may be included in corporate worship; what he has not commanded is forbidden, not merely permitted

Covenant theology — the Puritan framework: the covenant of works (Adam), the covenant of grace (Christ), applied through the domestic covenant of the Christian household under its head

Westminster Assembly (1643–1653) — the Puritan doctrinal apex: the Confession of Faith, Larger and Shorter Catechisms, the Directory for Public Worship — the fullest Reformed confessional statement ever produced

Banner of Truth Trust (est. 1957) — the twentieth-century recovery instrument: reprinting Owen, Watson, Flavel, Brooks, Sibbes, and the Puritans' complete works for a new generation of Reformed readers

Usage

"John Owen's Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656) applies Puritan spiritual discipline to the most practical Christian battle — the ongoing killing of indwelling sin by the Spirit's power — and remains the finest analysis of the internal Christian conflict in all of Reformed literature."

"The Puritans' theology of vocation — every calling (farming, trading, lawyering, homemaking) as an avenue of God-glorifying service — was a direct application of the Reformation's recovery of the priesthood of all believers to the whole of ordinary life, not just the ecclesiastical sphere."

"The Westminster Shorter Catechism's first question and answer — “What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever” — is the Puritan theological program in a single sentence: duty and delight, doxology and beatitude, are inseparable."
